questions.prompt: What is the main security takeaway about unencrypted network traffic?

options.text: Anything on the path (Wi-Fi, ISP, routers) can read or modify it
It is automatically protected by the Wi-Fi password
Only the destination server can see it
It cannot be intercepted once it leaves your device

questions.explanation: By default, unencrypted traffic is visible to anything along its path, which is why TLS/HTTPS is needed for anything private.

questions.prompt: Match each networking concept to its role.

pairs.right: Identifies an interface on the local link
Identifies which service a packet is for

questions.explanation: IP routes across networks, MAC reaches the local next hop, ports select the service, and DNS resolves names to addresses.

questions.prompt: Which statements about TCP and UDP are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: TCP begins with a three-way handshake
UDP is connectionless and fast with no delivery guarantee

questions.explanation: TCP is reliable and connection-oriented with a three-way handshake; UDP is connectionless and fast but makes no delivery or ordering guarantees.

questions.prompt: Order the TCP/IP layers from top (application) to bottom (link).
questions.explanation: The TCP/IP model runs Application, Transport, Internet, then Link; data is encapsulated as it moves down the stack.

questions.prompt: HTTPS uses TLS on port ____ by default.
questions.explanation: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) uses port 443, while plaintext HTTP uses port 80.

questions.prompt: Why does a Wi-Fi password NOT protect the contents of your browsing?

options.text: It controls access to the network, not the confidentiality of each site's traffic
It encrypts every website you visit end to end
It replaces the need for HTTPS
It hides your IP address from the destination

questions.explanation: A Wi-Fi password gates who can join the network; protecting the content of each connection requires HTTPS or a VPN.
